name: Game to Lose
description: Game to Lose is a three-player reverse trick-taking game from England's West Midlands. Players try to avoid taking valuable cards, because points are bad and the first player to 121 or more loses.
deck: Standard 52-card deck with one 13-card dummy hand each deal

overview.description: Game to Lose is a three-player reverse trick-taking game from England's West Midlands. Players try to avoid taking valuable cards, because points are bad and the first player to 121 or more loses.
overview.deck: Standard 52-card deck with one 13-card dummy hand each deal

history.origins: Game to Lose is documented as a West Midlands three-player reverse form of Chaser (Nine Card Don family).
timeline: Traditional Don and Chaser variants were widely played in English pub culture.
Game to Lose emerged as a local reverse-scoring adaptation for three active players.
Published modern rules preserve the crib-board race-to-lose format.
history.cultural: It belongs to the local Midlands all-fours and Don orbit of pub and workplace card games.
history.evolution: The main innovation is inversion of value: cards that would normally be desirable become penalties.

setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Rank high to low: A K Q J 10 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2.
setup.dealing: Dealer deals four clockwise 13-card hands one card at a time: pitcher, next player, dealer, and a dummy hand. The dummy hand is set aside face down as sleeping cards.
setup.equipment: Score pegs or cribbage board lanes are commonly used.

rules.objective: Avoid winning tricks that contain point-bearing cards. The first player to reach 121 points loses the match.
rules.gameplay: The pitcher leads to the first trick; the suit led becomes trump for the hand. Players must follow suit if able, otherwise may play any card. Highest card of led suit wins unless trump is played, then highest trump wins. Trick winner leads next trick. Points are pegged during play for certain trump cards and all fives; after all 13 tricks, card points are counted and the player with highest total pegs the Eight bonus.
keyRules: Trump is not preselected: it is set by the suit of the first card led by the pitcher.
A 13-card dummy hand is out of play each deal and can contain scoring cards.
If pegging from a trick takes a player to 121 or more, the game ends immediately and that player loses.

strategy.basic: Dump dangerous cards, especially fives and high trumps, when you can lose tricks safely.
strategy.intermediate: As pitcher, lead a suit where you are weak to avoid controlling too many early tricks.
strategy.advanced: Track opponent peg totals and force near-121 players into compulsory wins containing scoring cards.
tips: The 5 of trumps (10 points) and 9 of trumps (9 points) are the biggest immediate hazards.
Late in the hand, preserving low non-trumps can help you duck forced wins.

variations.name: Tie for Eight
variations.description: If two players tie for highest post-play card points, each pegs 4 instead of one player pegging 8.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Tie for Eight is a house rule; no engine constant overrides are needed for tie scoring.

scoring.description: Immediate pegging during trick play: trump A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1, 9=9, 5=10, and non-trump 5s=5 each. After 13 tricks, count A/K/Q/J/10 in won cards; highest count pegs 8 (or 4 each in a two-way tie).
scoring.winCondition: First player whose total reaches 121 or more loses.

synthesis.shortDescription: Three-player West Midlands reverse trick-taking game where taking valuable cards is bad.
